sources.quote: Currently, the form an is used before words starting with a vowel sound, regardless of whether the word begins with a vowel letter.

The past tense of the English verb 'run'.why: Deliberately false so the disjunction turns on the edited rule: the past tense of 'run' is 'ran'.

In the house style of the Zelbrask Gazet.why: A made-up class under a real one, the kind of thing that could exist unrecorded (coined jargon or a minor group, not a documented class), with made-up members named only in the prompts; it contradicts nothing written down. The rule gives the class the revision's new conclusion, the plural form.

In the Zelbrask Gazette's house style, i.why: Nobody writes about 'grimnet', a name made up for the prompt, so the direct sentence is not the kind of thing anyone says on its own; what people do say is the premise (that it is a zelbrask unit) and the general pattern, and only the inserted rule joins them. The made-up name makes the sentence unwritable elsewhere.

notes: Expansion paired with grammar-replace-0008 (a unit after a number in a hyphenated compound before a noun takes its plural form; relation takes_number_form and the new value, the plural form, are kept). Fictional subject: a made-up class of units newly defined in one craft's jargon (zelbrask units) under the real class 'unit of measurement', now restricted to the house style of a made-up trade journal, the Zelbrask Gazette. Nothing in real English leaves this slot open: every real unit takes the singular in such a compound (a ten-foot ladder), so a rule for real units would overwrite an inherited rule. A house style is a convention a publication may set for itself, so the closest non-conflicting expansion is a rule for one journal's style; real English is untouched. Derived queries name made-up units (grimnet, vorskin, brunzel) with the membership in the prompt. Near unrelated: the real unit 'foot' in standard English ('a ten-foot ladder'); a rule that leaks to all English gives 'ten-feet'.
